item.title: Trump praises Putin ahead of rare three-way meeting with Xi in China
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are about to hold talks in Shenzhen, China, a rare face-to-face meeting among the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries. Before that gathering, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin, and then Xi. The U.S. president and Putin spoke on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. "We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said while standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start." Cameras captured Mr. Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent entering a small conference room in Shenzhen to meet with Putin, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and other Russian officials. As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend." Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic they discussed, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood." Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way get-together. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States are "stable and improved." Mr. Trump told reporters he spoke with Xi for two hours on the APEC sidelines Wednesday, with trade and tariffs the main topics. He also noted he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite." He said he intends to discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi and Putin. Mr. Trump has said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with the three countries which, along with the United States, make up the world's three largest holders of nuclear weapons. But a range of other global challenges are lingering in the background, including the war in Iran and tensions over trade and artificial intelligence. The summit is taking place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China." Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing. Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire. Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence. "We do not want to do anything to destroy the tremendous potential of this technology," he said. "We have to watch it, we have to be careful, we have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements." Beyond AI, the U.S. and China have sought to stabilize their economic relationship over the last year, following a tit-for-tat trade war that sent tariffs above 100% in 2025. A tariff truce between the two countries is set to expire on Jan. 10 of next year. Mr. Trump said in his APEC speech the U.S. is committed to "growth and stability" in the Asia-Pacific region, and argued the American economy is "thriving like it has never thrived before." He also said the U.S. is negotiating "numerous trade agreements" and expects to sign some agreements with APEC members in the near future. During Xi's remarks earlier in the session, the Chinese leader called on countries in the region to "look out for each other" and "expand our shared interests," including on free trade and economic growth. Foreign conflicts loom large during the Trump-Putin-Xi talks. Iran is one contentious area, given China's status as one of the largest customers of Iranian oil, and Russia's ties with Iran. The White House previously said the war in Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said he expected the issue to come up, calling it "my favorite subject." Taiwan is another frequent discussion topic between the U.S. and China. During the U.S. president's visit to Beijing in the spring, Xi reportedly delivered a stern warning about the island , which he has long vowed to reintegrate with mainland China, floating potential "clashes and even conflicts" if the issue isn't "handled properly." And Mr. Trump was expected to press Xi to release two detained Americans during his visit to China, CBS News has reported . Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release. item.title: Democrats' sweeping midterm wins could reshape more than Trump's final 2 years
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
With Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska on Tuesday night , Democrats officially flipped their ninth U.S. Senate seat of the 2026 midterm elections — the most in nearly 70 years . When the next Congress takes office in early January, the Democratic Party will boast its largest Senate majority since 2011, with 56 seats to the GOP’s 44. Though a few races remain too close to call, the dust has mostly settled on Democrats’ 2026 landslide. Their sweeping victories in the U.S. House, Senate and statehouses nationwide add up to the biggest “blue wave” since Watergate . The question now is what Democrats plan to do with their newfound power. On Wednesday, the party nominated New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, putting him on track to be the first Black American to wield the gavel. With a majority that could top out at 260 seats after the last votes are counted — the largest for either party since the early 1990s — Jeffries will have enormous leeway to send new legislation to the Senate while also blocking parts of President Trump’s agenda, investigating his administration and possibly even impeaching him (again) . On the Senate side, Democratic stalwart Chuck Schumer of New York will compete with Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen for the role of majority leader. Whoever wins the party’s internal battle — which is expected to drag on for weeks — will control which policies are emphasized, which bills are brought to the floor, when votes occur, which judges and appointees are confirmed and how all of this is communicated to the president and the public. Among the priorities under discussion on both sides of the aisle: reinstating Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired under the previous Republican Congress; reversing nearly $1 trillion in recent GOP Medicaid cuts; expanding Medicare by lowering the eligibility age and adding vision, hearing and dental coverage; addressing the high prices of groceries and other goods by blocking Trump's global tariffs and restoring congressional power over trade policy; cutting off Iran war funding; and launching investigations of ICE, presidential pardons, political pressure on federal law enforcement, the Epstein files and the Trump family’s business dealings. As for impeachment, Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Democrat from Maryland who is set to chair the House Judiciary Committee, told Punchbowl that it’s a “critical tool in the constitutional toolbox” — but far from a sure thing. “We will not hesitate to use it if we think that the benefits exceed the costs," Raskin said. "But the one thing everybody's well aware of is that impeachment trials and impeachment motions soak up a lot of energy and oxygen." Despite their sizable House and Senate majorities, Democrats will be limited in what legislation they can pass into law. Trump still has veto power, and Senate Republicans still hold enough seats to filibuster most bills. Meanwhile, many incoming Democratic lawmakers (like Peltola) are relative moderates representing red states and districts — meaning the party will have to calibrate its approach carefully to keep them on board and maximize its chances of winning the 2028 elections. Beyond Washington, D.C., Democrats will now control the governorship and both legislative houses in six new states: Arizona, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Michigan and Minnesota. They will also hold the majority in a dozen new statehouse chambers. As a result, the party will have more opportunities to experiment with new policy ideas, approve congressional maps, influence election procedures, fill Senate vacancies and help a new generation of governors build executive experience ahead of future presidential elections. It’s even possible that state Democratic leaders could change the way we elect our next president by sidestepping the Electoral College and preventing candidates from winning the White House without winning the popular vote . How many Senate seats did Democrats win? Democrats came into the midterms needing a net gain of four seats to win back the Senate. To do that, they had to defend a handful of potentially vulnerable swing-state seats while also flipping at least a few seats in historically red states. That's exactly what happened. Republican efforts to flip blue seats in Michigan, Georgia, Minnesota and New Hampshire all came up well short. Meanwhile, Democrats won nine GOP-held seats in Mississippi, Maine, Texas, South Carolina, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and, as of Tuesday night, Alaska. Only two incumbent Republican senators in competitive races were able to win reelection: Florida's Ashley Moody and Nebraska's Pete Ricketts. The last undecided race was called late Tuesday night, as Mary Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan to become the first Alaska Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate since 2008. Peltola secured just over 50% of the vote, narrowly clearing the threshold required to win without triggering Alaska's unique ranked choice voting system. Democrats will enter 2027 with 56 seats in the Senate . How many House seats did Democrats win? So far, Democrats have won 257 U.S. House seats — far more than the 218 they needed for a majority. That includes 46 red-to-blue flips. Democrats' 14-point victory in the House popular vote is the largest in any midterm since 1974. Races that were too close to call on Election Night have been decided in the days that followed. Last Monday, incumbent GOP Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart of western Miami defeated Democratic challenger Nicole Locklin by about 1,700 votes in Florida's 26th Congressional District. Incumbent GOP Rep. Michael Baumgartner also won a tight race Monday in Washington's 5th Congressional District . Last Tuesday, incumbent Democrat Darren Soto — who was targeted by GOP redistricting efforts — defeated Republican challenger Dan Green by roughly 1,500 votes in central Florida's 9th District . Republican Ryan Elijah also defeated Democrat Bale Dalton by about 1,600 votes in Florida's 7th District around the same time. Both leads fell just outside recount requirements. In Florida's 27th District , incumbent Republican Maria Elvira Salazar defeated Democrat Eliott Rodriguez by just over 1,000 votes after a two-day recount. In California's 7th District , Democrat Doris Matsui won reelection, defeating Democratic challenger Mai Vang. Last Wednesday, incumbent Republican Joe Wilson won reelection in South Carolina's 2nd District by fewer than 3,000 votes. None of these seats were flipped. But on Thursday, Republicans did pick up Maine's 2nd District , where a conservative Democrat had retired — and where former GOP Gov. Paul LePage officially defeated Matt Dunlap, the progressive state auditor, by more than 5,000 votes after ranked-choice tabulation. Dunlap conceded to LePage on Nov. 5. On Friday, GOP firebrand Lauren Boebert lost her reelection battle in Colorado's 4th District — long considered one of the state's safest Republican seats — to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy. After a close 2022 reelection fight in her previous district, Boebert switched to the 4th District for her 2024 campaign and won by about 11 percentage points. Laubacher's lead — about 3,400 votes — was too big to trigger an automatic recount. Later Friday, Democrat Eric Jones unseated Democratic Rep. Mike Thompson in California's 4th District, where only Democrats were on the ballot under the state's top-two system. On Monday, Republican Reps. David Rouzer and Jay Obernolte narrowly won reelection to North Carolina's 7th District and California's 23rd District , respectively. Democrats flipped another GOP-held seat on Tuesday, when Raymond Smith was declared the winner in North Carolina's 3rd District. Smith prevailed by fewer than 300 votes. Where things stand in the undecided House races Seven U.S. House races remain unresolved. Two are in Louisiana, where the top two finishers in the 5th and 6th Districts will meet in a Dec. 12 runoff. As of Tuesday night, Democrats hold narrow leads in lead in races for three Republican-held seats. In Tennessee's 4th District , Victoria Broderick leads Rep. Scott DesJarlais by about 300 votes. In Minnesota's 1st District , Jake Johnson leads Rep. Brad Finstad by about 320 votes, and a recount is likely . In North Carolina’s 5th District , Chuck Hubbard leads Rep. Virginia Foxx by about 330 votes. Republicans lead in the other two: North Carolina's 10th and Alaska's at-large seat . In North Carolina, Democrat Ashley Bell requested a recount Friday after trailing Rep. Pat Harrigan by about 2,500 votes. North Carolina certifies results on Nov. 24. California certifies on Dec. 11. How many governorships did Democrats win? Republican governors have outnumbered their Democratic counterparts for the last 15 years straight (and for 26 of the last 30 years overall). But this year, Democrats have reversed the "governor gap," flipping six governorships in Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Nevada, Alaska and Georgia to bring their total to 30 — the party's first gubernatorial majority since 2011. On Thursday, Democrats also held onto Kansas , where voters elected Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher to become the Sunflower State's fourth woman governor ever. She defeated Republican Ty Masterson, the state's Senate president. "Kansans have sent a clear message that they want to keep our state moving forward," Holscher said in a video posted online Tuesday. "The work of preparing to lead has already begun." The AP called Alaska's governor race for Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins early Saturday. He won a majority of first-choice votes, so no ranked-choice count was needed. He will be the state's first Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office in 2002, and he takes office Dec. 7. How many state legislatures did Democrats win? Democrats' gains were also seen at the state level. They flipped more than 500 state legislative seats across the country and turned a total of 12 legislative chambers blue. That includes three states where they flipped both chambers: Arizona, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. After Election Day's results, Democrats will control the House, Senate and governorship in Arizona for the first time since 1966. Democrats also secured a "trifecta" in Wisconsin. They'll hold both legislative chambers in New Hampshire, but the governorship in the Granite State will remain in Republican hands. Democrats regained trifectas in Minnesota, Michigan and Pennsylvania by clinching majorities in the lone GOP-led chamber in their states. They flipped a single chamber in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, ensuring that Democratic governors in those states won't face unified Republican opposition within their state legislatures. Where things stand in the undecided state legislative races As of Monday morning, only three state legislative chambers — the North Carolina Senate and both chambers in Alaska — remained undecided, according to the AP. A recount is possible in North Carolina, where Senate control hinges on one race. item.title: Trump is trying to put the Iran war behind him, but it's not over
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
MANAMA, Bahrain - President Donald Trump appears eager to put the unpopular war with Iran behind him, as Democrats prepare to assume the majority on Capitol Hill after Republicans’ staggering midterm losses. But there is no indication that the war Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu started is anywhere near finished. The major issues of the conflict - control of the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. naval blockade, the fate of Iran’s nuclear program, Tehran’s support for regional proxies - remain unresolved. And Tehran’s perception of waning U.S. political will has left it emboldened. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Over the past week - following remarks by Trump at Arlington National Cemetery in which he said the war had been “won” - Iran three times has targeted the small nation of Bahrain, home to a massive U.S. naval base, with drones. On Wednesday it said it targeted a military base in Kuwait that is also home to U.S. forces in a drone and missile attack. The renewed Iranian strikes on Persian Gulf countries, the first in months, come as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels hit Saudi Arabia, and on top of severe economic damage wrought by Iran’s attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. In the strait, a vital waterway for the region’s oil shipments, videos verified by The Washington Post show tankers on fire and plumes of smoke billowing amid daily attacks this month. Iranian leaders, riding high on what they see as the U.S. voters’ rebuke of Trump in the midterms, show little sign of backing down. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament, warned in a speech on Sunday that the status quo of international economic pressure, which Trump has embraced as a key strategy to force eventual capitulation, is not sustainable. While Iran is open to negotiations if the United States accepts its demands, he said, Iran’s military “will determine the geography of the battlefield” if the U.S. “makes another mistake.” Both Iran and the U.S. “are scared of being seen as weak, and so they don’t want to make the first concession” in negotiations, said Abdulla Banndar Al-Etaibi, an assistant professor of international affairs at Qatar University. The two sides are so unpredictable, he said, that “anything is possible” in terms of escalation. “How can this be considered anything other than a victory for Iran?” asked Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, a Washington think tank. “The regime is surviving. The nuclear program is damaged but will be reconstituted, and they have realized what a jewel they have in terms of the Strait of Hormuz,” Vatanka said. “They will hold Gulf states hostage for years to come.” In response to requests for comment about ongoing violence in Hormuz and the resulting economic costs, the White House said in a statement that Iran is a “failed country” and that the U.S. “is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing.” Trump has said that a combination of a U.S. naval blockade and sanctions are crushing Iran’s economy and will force Iran to make a deal. The Trump administration has claimed that a massive U.S. military operation protecting vessels shuttling oil from the Persian Gulf into the Gulf of Oman, which launched in August, has helped get oil flows to prewar levels. But in the first 16 days of November, there were 16 attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy - following a record high of 37 attacks in October. In one of the most dramatic videos, posted on social media Nov. 8 and verified by The Post, a massive red Navig8 tanker is seen in flames near the coast of Oman as another boat sprays water on it. Satellite imagery captured by the European Space Agency satellite Sentinel-2 of the site of the attack shows a plume of smoke so large that it touches the shore. Oil spilled from damaged tankers has reached the shores of the United Arab Emirates and Oman, according to local media reports. Iranian state media has also reported that at least eight ships struck mines last week and over the weekend while traveling in waters that Iran considers restricted. U.S. Central Command posted a video Nov. 7 showing it firing “multiple precision munitions” at a commercial ship traveling in the Gulf of Oman that it said ignored U.S. warnings. The price of oil is down from record highs as the market has priced in the risk of travel through the strait, said Gregory Brew, a Middle East energy analyst with the consultancy Eurasia Group. But prices are still dramatically higher than before the war, he added, and overall traffic through the strait is a fraction of what it was before the war. “The Strait of Hormuz is neither open nor closed - it is contested,” Brew said. “The U.S. leaning back does not mean the war ends, especially for the Gulf.” The war has left the region mired in simmering conflict with no clear path to a decisive military outcome or broad peace agreement. In the early weeks of the war, when Iranian drones and missiles rained down on the Gulf, hitting hotels in Dubai, the U.S. military base in Bahrain and Qatar’s liquefied natural gas plant, Gulf officials publicly doubled down on their partnerships with the United States. Privately, many in the region bemoaned Trump’s decision to go to war and wondered whether the region would be left to pick up the pieces when he grew tired of the war they had warned him not to start. Nearly nine months in, with Trump saying the diplomatic solution sought by Qatar and backed by the rest of the Gulf is unnecessary, there is a sense of resignation. No one wants to publicly criticize Trump - the U.S. is still the Gulf’s main security guarantor - but speeches by top officials these days focus more on regional cooperation and expanding partnerships than the U.S. relationship. In interviews in recent weeks in Qatar, Bahrain and the UAE, residents said they felt both whiplash and a sense of hopelessness. Across the wealthy Gulf, nations have taken economic hits because of the war: The International Monetary Fund projects that gross domestic product will have contracted by an average of nearly 5 percent this year. But impact has been uneven, and most dramatically felt in Bahrain, Qatar and Kuwait, which do not have ports or any other viable options to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. In Qatar, which has long ranked as one of the world’s wealthiest countries by GDP per capita, state revenue dropped in the first half of the year by 42 percent, Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said last month. But the impact on everyday life has been limited, residents said. In Bahrain, an import-reliant island nation of 1.6 million that has far less oil and gas wealth than others in the region, the impact has been more acute. The country has seen its economy devastated by continued turmoil in Hormuz. Around the capital Manama on a recent day, storefront after storefront was shuttered, “for rent” signs in the windows. A supermarket manager said residents are only filling half their carts because of price hikes. Hair stylists said that their salon, empty on a recent Thursday afternoon, would have been bustling before the war. “I am nervous all the time,” said an artist. A steep drop in tourism forced him to close his shop. “It is the whole world that is suffering.” “We just want the U.S. to stop interfering,” said the artist, speaking on the condition of anonymity because of concerns about criticizing the U.S., a Bahraini ally. Sirens rang out across the country Sunday morning and again on Tuesday, as Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said its drones were targeting U.S. military equipment. The government once again warned residents to seek shelter. Bahrain’s media office said in a statement that the country had been “subjected to repeated and unjustifiable Iranian attacks on its territory.” As the sun set and a group of men prepared to head to the mosque for evening prayers, they bemoaned the situation. Abdul Aziz said that he used to make a living importing motorbikes and bicycles that he sold to U.S. soldiers at the naval base in Bahrain. Now, he said, goods that used to take a month to arrive are taking four. The Americans he used to sell to are gone - thousands of them evacuated from the base ahead of the war. The market, he said, “has died because of the war and because of Hormuz.” “I don’t know until when we will suffer,” he said. “But we just want things to be normal again.” George and Steckelberg reported from Washington, and Piper from London. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/18/trump-is-trying-put-iran-war-behind-him-its-not-over/

item.title: 'GTA 6' reviews are in after a 13-year wait, and critics are going bananas
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The much-anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here, and critics who have spent weeks playing it before the public say it's worth the hype. The open-world format allows gamers to explore Vice City, the sun-drenched fictional Miami-like metropolis in the Florida-like state of Leonida, as the Bonnie-and-Clyde-like criminal duo Jason and Lucia. "Rockstar's Vice City is a masterpiece I never want to leave," PC Mag's Jordan Minor wrote in his review . " Grand Theft Auto VI is simply one of the best-looking video games I've ever seen." He wasn't alone. "Unprecedented. Unbelievable. Unmissable," declared IGN's Luke Reilly . "This is a world that feels more lived-in and real than anything I've ever played." View this post on Instagram Same for the Guardian's Keza MacDonald , who gave it a glowing review . "In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen," MacDonald wrote, adding: "Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it's hard to know where to start." Here's what other top gaming critics are saying about GTA VI. Lucia and Jason in a scene from Grand Theft Auto VI . Rockstar Games Yussef Cole, the New York Times : This is a game about love and relationships, their joy and heartache, and the work required to make them successful. The surprising depth to which these themes are explored makes for a memorable and endearing experience in Grand Theft Auto VI, which largely lives up to its sky-high expectations by inverting the series's reputation for destruction. Zack Zwiezen, Kotaku : The best part of Grand Theft Auto 6 isn't what I expected. It's not the crime, or the action, or the massive world to explore, though all of those parts are excellent and better than ever. The real standout of GTA 6 , the part of the game that kept me hooked and which I won't forget anytime soon, is its central duo, Jason and Lucia. Not only do they have very different motivations than past GTA protagonists, wanting to create a better life for themselves and escape their life of crime instead of vying to become crime lords or get revenge, but they are easily Rockstar's most fully fleshed-out, believable, and relatable characters. View this post on Instagram Giovanni Colantonio, Polygon : Through Jason and Lucia's genuine chemistry, GTA 6 gives you a better reason to work through Leonida's daily grind. Yes, there's always another bank to rob or car to steal, but that's not the reason you wake up in the morning. It's to prove that love can survive in a cruel culture that tries so hard to beat it out of people. So be it if you have to play dirty to keep pace with the cold-hearted crooks who make their fortune from someone else's pain. It shouldn't be this hard to settle down with your lover and enjoy a sunset together in the rotten social climate that Rockstar has been eager to lampoon for decades at this point. People will hem and haw about Grand Theft Auto's purported glamorization of lawlessness. They always have; they always will. But it will be different this time. GTA 6 's empathy is bound to be the most controversial thing about it. Lucia and Jason in another scene from "Grand Theft Auto VI." Rockstar Games Kyle Orland, ArsTechnica : The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you'd expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers. But it's the scenes between the over-the-top and somewhat repetitive action scenes that really make this Grand Theft Auto stand out. Almost every explosive gunfight or high-speed car chase is counterpointed by a sublimely dull, lightly interactive moment of mere routine existence: grilling burgers with pals by the water, playing fetch with a random dog, helping a neighbor tune up a car, or joking around over 18 holes of mini golf. Taken together, the juxtaposition lends a sense of surreal hyperreality to the goings-on in Vice City and its environs. Each of the game's two sides gives the other a chance to breathe, forming a series of emotional peaks and valleys that stretch across a truly gargantuan amount of detailed simulation and pure gaming content. Grand Theft Auto VI never lets you get too settled with a budding life of crime or a budding family life. And it's all the better for it. Running from the law is, of course, part of "GTA 6." Rockstar Games Gene Park, The Washington Post : After enough years of playing games, you know what to expect. You recognize the tricks, anticipate the limits and learn which doors will never open. Other games are still immensely entertaining, but you stop wondering. "Grand Theft Auto VI" brings the wonder back. I wanted to speak to everyone, follow every street and open every door. My experience with games kept telling me where the possibilities could end. Then "GTA VI" would do something that would shock and delight. Writing about this game feels like sending dispatches from the future. I've been desperate to tell people what happened there, as if I've returned from a new life. Tamoor Hussain, GameSpot : Only Rockstar commands the time and money necessary to make a game as dedicated to small details. And only Rockstar can execute on the realizing [of] such a granular vision unimpeachably. The obsession with the minutiae both explains and justifies the 13-year wait. This game is the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach. GTA 6 is an astonishing open-world action game that I'd wager won't be outdone until Grand Theft Auto 7 . item.title: Costco sees surge in panic buying after a string of tech outages, report says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Consumers are panic-buying at Costco, snapping up generators and other emergency-preparedness items in response to a recent string of technology outages , according to investment firm Mizuho Securities. "Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a report. Shoppers are "pantry-loading," while 21 of the retailer's 26 "high-ticket generators" were sold out online as of Sunday night, he added. The recent outages, which blocked access to Microsoft apps , snarled flights nationwide and hindered banking activities at various times during the past week, are raising questions among Americans about a larger cybersecurity threat, CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman said on "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday. The companies affected by the outages have said they were due to issues such as routine maintenance or upgrades, while the Federal Aviation Administration blamed its nationwide ground stop last week on a contractor updating its flight system. "All of them have denied that cyberattacks are to blame," Gutman said. "Still, the system failures are fueling online speculation about a larger cyber threat." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that there's "zero evidence" that the recent outages in the U.S. are linked. "The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA . The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we've seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another," Rubio said during a news conference in the Philippines. Costco didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The close timing of the outages highlights the country's increasing reliance on technology, John D'Arcy, a Temple University professor who researches cybersecurity and information technology failures, told CBS News Philadelphia. "Our systems are so much more complex and so much more interconnected than they ever have been in the past, that when we just have one failure, the effects are much more dramatic," D'Arcy said. The surge in panic buying could lift Costco's sales, Bellinger wrote. He raised his target price for the company's stock to $1,150 from $1,100. Other big-box stores, including Walmart and Sam's Club, could see similar "pantry-loading lifts," he added. item.title: 'There was no monitoring': Sources dispute FAA oversight of work before ground stop
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Passengers wait at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA), in Arlington, Virginia, just outside Washington, DC, on November 14. - Aaron Scwartz/AFP/Getty Images On the morning of last week’s historic nationwide ground stop , an FAA technician escorted a private contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control centers in south Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician believed his role ended when the contractor entered the facility. He went about his own work without knowing exactly what the L3Harris engineer was doing, according to two sources familiar with what happened in the room, and the union that represents FAA technicians. Not long after it was replaced, that new router triggered a cascade of communications problems, flooding the FAA’s aging network with data and leading the FAA to take the rare step later that day of issuing a full nationwide ground stop. About 3,500 planes were in the air when departures were halted for more than four hours while the agency worked to figure out the problem. The details of how that router was installed and who was overseeing that work is now in dispute and emerging as a key point of tension in unraveling what exactly went wrong that day. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has defended the FAA’s modernization process and insisted that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was done beforehand. But sources who spoke to CNN dispute this characterization. The technician “was only there to unlock the door,” one of them said. “There was no monitoring,” another source said. That kind of hands-off arrangement, sources say, is a recent development and represents a stark change from how this kind of maintenance work was handled by previous administrations, when the FAA typically exercised far more oversight of contractors’ work. A crucial memo from March 2025 But in an effort to speed up and streamline the modernization of the nation’s air traffic control system with $12.5 billion from President Donald Trump’s “big beautiful bill,” the administration diminished FAA oversight of this kind of work, the sources said. In a memo dated March 2025, the FAA laid out some key changes to how maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, noting: “It is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.” Under the policy change, the FAA shifted from receiving maintenance “requests” from its private contractors to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” according to the memo. Airplanes are parked on the tarmac after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" following the agency's earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, on November 13. - Jonathan Ernst/Reuters The memo does note that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, but the sources told CNN there are only a handful of liaisons nationwide processing thousands of notifications. “So what level of oversight are they really doing?” one of the sources said. As a result, the L3Harris contractor at the center of Friday’s outage showed up with just a few days’ notice and conducted the work without any meaningful oversight from the agency, according to the sources and the union. The March 2025 memo “laid the groundwork for what happened last Friday,” the source said. “They’re not requesting to go out anymore. They’re just notifying and going and then they’re doing the work,” the source said. “And that circumvents the operational risk management aspect where the technician before who works for the government could say, no, no. You can’t do that right now.” Elizabeth Doherty, a spokeswoman for the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union that represents FAA technicians, told CNN the technician’s “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.” CNN asked the FAA about the discrepancy over whether an FAA technician was or was not providing real time oversight of the work. “There is a lot of information that we’re trying to track down. So things have been changing,” FAA spokeswoman Hannah Walden told CNN by phone. “It could have been a misunderstanding or whatever. So I’m not saying one way or the other right now. I just am saying we’re trying to provide information as we get it.” In addressing the changes laid out in the 2025 memo, Walden denied oversight has been reduced, saying the policy change “does not change oversight at all. It changes the priority of the work that needs to be done.” After this story published, Walden sent an additional statement, seeming to contradict what Bedford said publicly on Tuesday about the technician monitoring the upgrade. “The FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building. Because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work,” she said in the statement. The episode underscores the complications that can arise over a communications system that is operated by the federal government yet is owned by a private company, in this case L3Harris, whose telecom network serves as the communications backbone for the nation’s airspace. It also comes as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is asking Congress to approve another $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control system even as lawmakers question how the billions allocated last year were spent. L3Harris declined to provide any details in response to CNN’s questions. In a statement to CNN, the company said it is “supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel.” People sit on the floor as they wait to try and retrieve luggage during delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City. - Adam Gray/Getty Images A routine job, then chaos The policy change laid out in the March 2025 memo didn’t come out of nowhere. The sources familiar with what happened before the ground stop said a chronic, yearslong shortage of FAA technicians as well as the Trump administration’s push for speed helped propel it forward. The result, they believe, was less oversight of the contractor on Friday and a much slower recovery, as the FAA struggled to pinpoint the source of the problem. L3Harris notified the FAA on November 9 that it planned to carry out maintenance, replacing a router, at a remote FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, with work set to begin at 9 a.m. on Friday, November 13, one of the sources said. Four days after the notice, the L3Harris worker arrived. Even the time of day the work was scheduled raised eyebrows, given it was at a time of heavy air traffic. The sources say FAA technicians were not consulted about the best time to carry out this work at this facility. By that Friday afternoon, the new router was connected and the L3Harris contractor had left the site with no idea of the chaos that was beginning to unfold, the source said. Hours later, FAA technicians got a call telling them to return to the site to escort the L3Harris engineer back into the facility. The agency scrambled to find the closest available staff to let him in. Hours had passed between the time the engineer had left and the time he returned to retrieve the router, the source said. A former FAA technician told CNN that, for agency technicians, checking in with air traffic controllers before leaving a site is standard practice. It’s not clear if the L3Harris engineer took this step. “As a technician, anytime when I was out there … and I did anything, anything at all to the equipment before I left, I would call up the TRACON or the center or the tower, whatever controllers that had the services that I was providing on that equipment. And I would say, ‘I’m getting ready to leave. Everything look good? Everything okay? You got everything?’ They’d be like, ‘yep,’” the former technician said. “It’s just a practice that you do.” In the immediate aftermath of the ground stop, Duffy was sharply critical of L3Harris, making a point of calling them out in his public remarks. “We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job,” Duffy said during his Saturday press conference. “Many of our contractors, many or our partners, they take our money and they provide really poor service to us. Full stop.” Yet by Tuesday, Bedford sounded a different tone toward L3Harris. At a news conference, Bedford described the L3Harris contractor who replaced the router as a “highly trained certified engineer, former Air Force veteran, I’m told a generally competent guy doing the work that he has done dozens and dozens of times before.” Asked what oversight the FAA provides when contractors work at FAA facilities, Bedford also said, “There is a comprehensive risk management process with every installation. And that installation happens whether it’s with a contractor or with an FAA employee.” Days earlier, Duffy had defended the timing of the work, pointing out that it was at a remote location. He said he didn’t expect the kind of impact seen last Friday at “smaller locations.” This story has been updated with additional details. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/18/politics/faa-contractor-oversight-ground-stop

item.title: Republican senator blocks Trump's judicial nominee as Democrats prepare to take over
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Nate Raymond and David Morgan WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's efforts to secure Senate confirmation of as many conservative judges as possible before Democrats take control of the chamber suffered a setback on Wednesday after ‌a Republican senator blocked one of his nominees from advancing. Outgoing Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas withheld support for US ‌Department of Justice official T. Elliot Gaiser to appear before the Senate Judiciary Committee for a hearing on Wednesday where it could take up his nomination to be a ​federal judge in Dallas. Cornyn's decision not to return a so-called blue slip backing Gaiser marked the latest instance of a Republican senator not supporting a White House-backed judicial nominee in their home state during the lame-duck session before Democrats take control of the Senate on January 3. "He's not from Texas," Cornyn told Reuters. "He has no trial experience, and the White House was trying to jam him down our throat without adequate ‌vetting for a lifetime job." A White House official ⁠in a statement said it expects all of Trump's judicial nominees to be confirmed by year's end. Senators traditionally help choose nominees for vacancies on federal courts in their states. By Senate custom, they can effectively veto ⁠trial court nominees they oppose in their states by refusing to return a blue slip, a form used to signal support. Trump nominated Gaiser, 37, to a seat on the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas after the election. The former Ohio solicitor general previously clerked for conservative US ​Supreme ​Court Justice Samuel Alito and currently heads the Justice Department's Office of ​Legal Counsel, a key unit that has frequently signed ‌off on the legality of his administration's actions. Cornyn, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger, during Wednesday's hearing expressed support for Trump's decision to separately nominate Texas Supreme Court Justice James Sullivan to serve as a federal judge after he was defeated by a Democrat in the recent election. But Cornyn has been pushing for the White House to pick someone else for the seat Gaiser was nominated to fill, recommending instead former federal prosecutor Steve Fahey of Texas. "And the White House now seems to ‌be showing some interest in that," Cornyn said in an interview. Republican Senator Ted ​Cruz of Texas, who supports Gaiser, in a statement warned that the White ​House has indicated that it would be "impossible for a brand-new ​nominee to complete the FBI background check fast enough to be confirmed." "If the Senate Judiciary Committee does not ‌move Gaiser forward, the people of Texas will pay ​the price because it will effectively ​give the judicial seat to the Democrats, who will keep it vacant in perpetuity," Cruz said. Two of Trump's other judicial nominees similarly ran into resistance from Republican senators in their home states after the midterm elections. The White House on November 10 rescinded ​US District Judge Lee Rudofsky's nomination to the ‌8th US Circuit Court of Appeals and nominated Arkansas Supreme Court Justice J. Cody Hiland in his place following opposition ​from Arkansas' Republican senator. Hiland appeared at Wednesday's hearing with six other nominees. (Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston and ​David Morgan in Washington; Editing by Bill Berkrot and Alistair Bell) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/republican-senator-cornyn-blocks-trump-173537955.html

item.title: Musk says he feels 'foolish' after spending over $440 million to back Republicans
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, expressed buyer’s remorse Wednesday about his massive — and ultimately futile — spending spree to elect Republicans in the midterms. The SpaceX and Tesla founder, who spent over $440 million backing GOP candidates, most of whom lost, acknowledged: “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.” The comments came during The New York Times’ DealBook Summit, where Musk also distanced himself from President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement, maintaining “there are positives and negatives in both parties.” “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much. Or maybe it would have been much worse without that,” Musk said at the event, which he attended virtually from China, as he and other business leaders accompanied President Donald Trump to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. “But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money.” Musk, who has experienced an on-again off-again relationship with Trump, was by far the biggest single donor this election cycle, spending at an unprecedented clip to support Republicans. But his efforts failed to make a major impact, as key GOP strongholds such as Texas, where he spent the bulk of his money, and Kansas flipped to Democrats. Despite his midterm spending, Musk sought to clarify during Wednesday’s public interview that he is “not MAGA” — regardless of his ties with the president. Instead, Musk claimed he supported a balance of power between Democrats and Republicans in the government. “I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that,” Musk said. These statements conflict with how Musk aligned with Trump in the past, even going as far to label himself as “Dark MAGA” when he campaigned for him just two years ago. In fact, Musk appeared optimistic about working with the newly elected Democratic governor in Texas, where he runs massive SpaceX and Tesla operations. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has criticized the tech billionaire, has also said she is open to a “strong working relationship” with Musk. “The new governor, actually, I think, is going to be quite moderate,” Musk said. “I don’t think she’s sort of a far-left governor. And based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/18/musk-says-he-feels-foolish-after-gop-election-spending-spree-01174509

item.title: The lead actress in 'GTA 6' once feared playing a 'damsel in distress.' Then came this role.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
There are a lot of things players can do in Grand Theft Auto VI that weren't possible in previous editions of the franchise. One of the most notable is that they can play as Lucia, the first major female protagonist in the history of the series. Iconic female main characters have been a staple of video games from the beginning (see: Ms. Pac-Man, Samus Aran, etc.), but the presence of a complex, fully fleshed-out woman at the core of GTA 6 's story represents a significant change for a franchise that has been accused in the past of treating female side characters as equal parts eye candy and cannon fodder. In the lead-up to the game's release, most of its sprawling cast of voice actors had remained a mystery. That's still true of nearly all of its main characters. But the voice behind Lucia was seemingly confirmed on Tuesday when the Game Awards announced that Manni L. Perez had been nominated for Best Performance for her voice work in the game. GTA 6 received eight nominations in total, including Game of the Year. The revelation came as little surprise to die-hard GTA fans, who had speculated for months that the little-known American actor was the voice behind one half of the game's core duo. GTA 6 's story centers around Lucia and her boyfriend Jason, a pair of outlaws trying to make their mark in a cartoonishly criminal knockoff of Miami called Vice City. The actor who plays Jason is still unknown. Who is Manni L. Perez? The limited information we have about Perez's personal bio comes from her own recent social media statements and a few dated news stories. While deftly dodging a deluge of questions from GTA fans asking her to confirm her role in the game on Instagram Live last month, she described herself as having grown up in a "small, rural, rednecky hick town" roughly three hours from New York, where she now lives. "We grew up very lower middle class," she added. She said she has family in Harlem and is reportedly of Puerto Rican and Dominican descent. According to a 2018 interview with Paz Magazine, Perez studied at New York University's prestigious Tisch School of the Arts. She said she initially wanted to pursue a career as a professional belly dancer before being convinced to try acting by a college professor. Perez is also an avid weightlifter and has practiced a variety of martial arts, including Muay Thai and Brazilian jiu-jitsu. "I have a very specific niche in the industry," she told the magazine. "A lot of the roles I get called in for require me to be fit, strong, and kick ass." Perez has played a series of minor TV roles in recent years, including guest appearances on J essica Jones , Chicago P.D. and Law & Order: Special Victims Unit . On Instagram, she told her followers that her modest acting success so far hasn't yet fundamentally changed her life. "I live in a small studio apartment, which I love," she said. "I have my tiny, little itty-bitty kitchen, and it's just me and my dog. I do everything on my own, and I've done everything on my own for a very long time, and I love it, and I'm very grateful." GTA 6 is her breakout role, but it isn't the first work she's done with the franchise. She was credited as the voice of Clubber #2 in Grand Theft Auto V and as an unnamed blackjack dealer in a 2019 update to Grand Theft Auto Online . One comment Perez made to Paz Magazine eight years ago turned out to be remarkably prescient about the role that would turn into a major star in the video game world. "To be honest, my biggest fear is to play a woman that needs to be saved by a man," she said. "Like, I can't imagine playing the damsel in distress. … I'd prefer to play a character that, whatever she's going through, no matter how hard society wants to keep her down, she picks herself up, puts her big girl panties on (preferably cotton) and keeps it moving." What do we know about the rest of the cast? Very little. Fans have speculated that Lucia's partner, Jason Duval, is played by actor Dylan Rourke , who's appeared in Grey's Anatomy and Modern Family , but Rockstar has not confirmed that. More rumors abound about the other actors who voice the game's key characters, but so far only one other cast member has been officially announced. Celebrated comedic actor Stephen Root , who recently won an Emmy for his supporting role on Widow's Bay , has confirmed that he'll play a criminal named Brian Heder, who GTA 6's character guide describes as "a classic drug runner from the golden age of smuggling." item.title: Army's planned detonation in Iowa raises concerns over lead exposure
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Residents in parts of southeastern Iowa and northwest Illinois are being warned about possible lead dust exposure as the U.S. Army prepares to detonate 68 barrels of lead azide that have been stored for more than 20 years at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. The barrels cannot be safely transported because the lead azide had become drier and more volatile than expected, according to Justine Barati, deputy chief of public and congressional affairs for Army Sustainment Command. The aging explosive can detonate from movement, friction or other disturbances, and Army officials determined that an on-site detonation was the safest disposal option. The detonation, scheduled for Nov. 20, is expected to generate two rapid explosions and ground vibrations that could potentially damage windows, according to an Army public advisory . Army air-dispersion modeling showed a potential airborne lead plume extending close to 100 miles from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Officials have advised residents within the projected impact area to evacuate beforehand if possible or remain indoors with windows closed and ventilation systems set to recirculate air. The Army and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency say air sampling, environmental monitoring and post-detonation cleanup efforts are planned. Officials have maintained that the blast should result in temporary and limited environmental impacts. But the operation has raised concerns among health and environmental experts, who question whether the Army has released enough information about potential lead exposure. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is located near Middletown, a small town in southeastern Iowa's Des Moines County near the Illinois border. 'A geyser of debris': What we know about air quality following LA area landfill gas release Potential lead exposure risks The Army has released plume maps showing where lead particles could travel after the blast, raising concerns among residents and health experts. Depending on weather conditions, the plume could extend across portions of southeastern Iowa and northwest Illinois. Jennifer Sample, a medical toxicologist, told the USA TODAY Network's Des Moines Register that lead remains particularly dangerous for young children because it can cause irreversible neurological damage. While some schools have already canceled classes on Nov. 20 in anticipation of the detonation, Sample said "the state of Iowa should close all schools in the plume path." A brief exposure to low concentrations is not the same as months or years of exposure and does not necessarily result in lead poisoning. However, health experts note that there is no scientifically established threshold below which lead exposure is entirely risk-free. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , no safe blood lead level has been identified in children. Even low levels of exposure can affect learning, attention and academic performance. Experts also warn that lead can accumulate in adults' bones over time. During pregnancy and breastfeeding, lead can be released along with calcium and pass to the fetus or infant. How to protect yourself from lead exposure In its public safety advisory , the Army warned that exposure could occur through inhalation of airborne lead particles or contact with lead dust that settles on surfaces. Officials recommend that people in potentially affected areas: Remain indoors during the potential exposure period if they cannot evacuate beforehand. Close all windows, exterior doors, and other openings during the exposure period. Turn off or place heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems in recirculation mode, minimize outdoor air intake, and maximize indoor air filtration during the potential exposure period. Avoid traveling through the affected area during the potential exposure period. Wet-clean surfaces that may be contacted by children, including outdoor play equipment, toys, tables and chairs, handrails, patios, decks, exterior windowsills and other high-contact surfaces. Pet owners should take precautions as well. Sample said dogs allowed outside could carry lead dust back into homes and should be washed before returning indoors. She also said wildlife could be exposed to lead particles and absorb lead into their bodies. Independent researchers express skepticism While Army officials said the environmental impacts should be minor and short-term, some independent researchers remain skeptical. Drew Latta, director of Iowa's "Get the Lead Out" program, said information about the detonation should have been released to the public sooner. "It just seems like there's a lot of unease. And if they've got evidence that can cause that unease to go away, they need to do better at communicating it. And quickly," Latta told the Register . David Cwiertny, director of the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination at the University of Iowa, also expressed reservations about the Army's cleanup plans, writing on social media that hosing down lead-containing dust does not mean it is "magically gone." Latta and Cwiertny have been working together to conduct independent monitoring research of the detonation. 'Credible threat': Illinois man charged after bomb threat at Peoria ethanol plant US Army says detonation is safest option Lead azide is a primary explosive used to initiate munitions, according to a Q&A sheet from the plant . The barrels had been moved to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant for use in munitions production but were not all used, Barati said. The material was later designated hazardous waste, and the facility shut down for two weeks in March to conduct a safety review out of an abundance of caution. Army officials say leaving the material in storage presents growing risks, particularly during colder weather. "It's the Army trying to do the best and safest thing for the public, because we are concerned that as the weather gets colder, lead azide becomes more volatile — and it could self detonate," Barati told the Register. Responding to concerns about lead contamination, Barati said projected exposures would be minimal and temporary. She also confirmed there are no plans to offer lead blood testing related to the detonation. "It's not lead paint where it's a chronic exposure by children," she said. "It's the equivalent of living in a mining town for one hour." Residents whose property is damaged by the blast may submit claims to the Army, and some property owners may be asked to allow environmental sampling on their land. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Army's planned detonation in Iowa raises concerns over lead exposure This article originally appeared on USA TODAY at https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2026/11/18/iowa-army-ammunition-plant-lead-azide-detonation/92852446007/
